One such instance that comes to mind is my decision to support the Kansas-Nebraska Act in 1854. At the time, I believed in the principle of popular sovereignty, allowing the residents of a territory to decide on the issue of slavery for themselves. However, the repercussions of that decision became clearer as the violent conflicts in Kansas escalated, and I came to see the flaws in that approach.

When I realized the mistake I had made, I did not shy away from acknowledging it. I publicly admitted my error and worked to rectify it by speaking out against the spread of slavery into new territories. I believe that true leadership requires the humility to admit when one is wrong and the courage to take corrective action.

In facing challenges and defeats, I have always strived to learn from my mistakes and emerge stronger and more determined. I believe that my experiences have shaped me into a candidate who is committed to principles over expediency, and who will always stand firm in the face of adversity.
